app.title: Orrery — three models of the solar system
app.subtitle: Ptolemy · Copernicus · Newton
mode.label: Model
engine.label: Construction
engine.help.ptolemaic-reframe: Accurate positions expressed with Earth at the centre. What Ptolemy was approximating.
engine.help.ptolemaic-epicyclic: Ptolemy's actual construction with Almagest parameters, errors included.
engine.help.circular: The heliocentric model with perfectly circular orbits, as Copernicus published it in 1543. Ellipses arrived only with Kepler in 1609 — which is why this model predicts the superior planets less well than Ptolemy does.
engine.help.nbody: Numerical integration of Newton's law of gravity. Orbits are not prescribed; they emerge — and what emerges is Kepler's ellipses, now as a consequence rather than an assumption.
ghost.label: Compare with
ghost.hint: A second model is drawn faintly beside the active one.
frame.label: Stationary point
frame.hint: Which body is held at the centre of the map.
observer.label: Observation point
observer.hint: Where the sight-lines to the celestial sphere start from.
time.label: Time
harness.label: Overlays
harness.sightlineBend: The sight-line bends at the body because the compressed scale distorts angles measured from anywhere but the centre of the map. At true scale the bend all but disappears; in Ptolemy's view, where Earth is also the centre, the line is perfectly straight.
harness.trailsEmpty: Orbits are drawn from positions actually visited, not computed in advance. Run the clock and the trail builds.
harness.trailsRecorded: {{days}} days recorded, {{step}}-day steps. Longer history is kept more coarsely.
view.scaleHint: Compressed scale shows every orbit at once; true scale keeps the distance ratios honest.
view.zodiac.label: Zodiac
view.constructionHint: Select a body to see its machinery — circles for Ptolemy and Copernicus, force vectors for Newton.
view.constructionLegend: The thin circle is the deferent, the heavier one the epicycle. The open ring marks the deferent's centre; the diamond marks the equant, the point about which the epicycle's centre moves uniformly. The dashed line is the apsidal axis.
view.constructionScaleWarning: At compressed scale the circles appear distorted. Switch to true scale to see them as the circles they are.
info.title: Selected body
info.none: Select a body on the map.
events.title: Events
events.comparison.title: When each model predicts this event
locale.label: Language
info.forceScaleNote: Vector lengths are ordered but not proportional — the Sun is over 98% of the pull, so true proportions would leave the others invisible. Exact figures are in the table.
view.forcesLegend: The blue vector is velocity, the black one the net force. The thin vectors are each body's gravitational pull, coloured by which body pulls. Lengths are ordered, not proportional — exact figures are listed under the selected body.
view.sphere.frameHint: The celestial sphere is concentric with the map, as on a traditional orrery. Sight-lines bend at the body when the observer is not the centre.
view.sphere.observerHint: The celestial sphere surrounds the observation point, which is where the sky actually belongs. Sight-lines are then straight in every model; the sphere is no longer concentric with the map, and the map shrinks to make room.
theme.label: Look
view.zoomHint: The mouse wheel zooms the map, always about the stationary point. Double-click the map to return to the fitted view.
engine.help.ptolemaic-almagest: The same construction driven by Ptolemy's own mean motions and his precession — what a second-century astronomer would actually have computed. His rates are excellent, but the error is paid once per revolution: over nineteen centuries the outer planets drift about a degree, Venus and Mercury by tens.
events.comparison.referenceNote: Reference from the VSOP87 theory, times in UT. Within minutes of published values — under ten for both the 2020 Mars opposition and the great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn.
engine.help.vsop87: VSOP87, the analytical theory used here as the reference. Elliptical orbits with their mutual perturbations; the yardstick the three historical models are measured against.
